body:
Farmers are more than purchasers of seeds

Farmers cultivate crops, select seeds, preserve varieties and often maintain locally adapted plant material over many generations. Some farmers also develop new varieties. The PPV&FR Act recognises these different roles because plant improvement depends not only on formal breeding programmes but also on the continuing conservation and use of agricultural genetic resources.

The right to save and use seeds

Section 39(1)(iv) allows a farmer to save, use, sow, resow, exchange, share or sell farm produce, including seed of a protected variety, in the same manner as the farmer was entitled to do before the Act came into force.

There is a decisive exception: a farmer is not entitled to sell branded seed of a variety protected under the Act. For this purpose, the Act describes branded seed as seed placed in a package or other container and labelled in a way indicating that it is a protected variety.

The right to use or exchange farm-saved seed does not create an unrestricted right to undertake commercial seed multiplication and market packaged branded seed of a protected variety.

For example, a farmer cultivating a protected variety may ordinarily retain part of the harvested produce for sowing and exchange farm produce as permitted by law. Selling packaged seed marketed under the protected variety's name is different and falls outside this particular farmer exemption.

Farmers as breeders and conservers

Under section 39(1)(i), a farmer who breeds or develops a new variety is entitled to seek registration and protection like any other breeder, subject to the law's requirements, with exclusive rights to produce, sell, market, distribute, import or export the registered variety. Section 39(1)(ii) also recognises registration of farmers' varieties.

Farmers who conserve landraces and wild relatives of economically important plants may receive recognition and rewards from the National Gene Fund under section 39(1)(iii), provided the statutory conditions are satisfied. In particular, the material selected and preserved must have been used as a source of genes in a variety registrable under the Act.

A landrace is a traditionally maintained, locally adapted plant population or variety developed over time through cultivation and selection. Conserving such material can be valuable because it preserves genetic diversity that may later help breeding programmes.

Benefit sharing for contributions to breeding

A breeder may create a commercially useful variety by using genetic material conserved by a farming or local community. The Act recognises that the contribution of this material may justify a share in the benefits.

Under section 26, after registration of a variety the Authority invites benefit-sharing claims. Claims may be submitted by Indian citizens or groups of Indian citizens, or by firms and governmental or non-governmental organisations formed or established in India. The breeder is given an opportunity to respond, and the Authority determines any benefit-sharing amount after considering the extent and nature of the claimant's genetic contribution and the commercial usefulness and demand of the registered variety.

Any benefit-sharing amount determined under the provision is deposited by the breeder into the National Gene Fund for the purposes specified by law. The Fund also supports conservation and sustainable use of genetic resources.

Rights of village and local communities

Section 41 separately enables a claim on behalf of a village or local community that has significantly contributed to the evolution of a registered variety. A qualifying person, group or organisation may file the claim at a centre notified by the Authority with the Central Government's prior approval; the centre verifies the contribution and reports its findings to the Authority. The Authority may order compensation after the required verification, notice and hearing.

Section 40 requires applicants for variety registration to disclose the use of genetic material conserved by tribal or rural families. This helps make relevant community contributions visible during the registration process.

Compensation when seeds fail to perform as claimed

Section 39(2) addresses a different situation. When propagating material of a registered variety is sold to farmers, its breeder must disclose the expected performance under given conditions. If the material fails to provide that performance under those conditions, the affected farmers may claim compensation before the Authority.

The Authority gives the breeder notice and an opportunity to contest the claim, hears the parties and may order appropriate compensation. Compensation is not automatic whenever a crop fails. The claimed performance, specified growing conditions, evidence and statutory procedure matter.

Other protections worth knowing

Section 42 protects a farmer from infringement liability when the farmer proves that, at the time of the infringement, the farmer was unaware of the existence of the protected right. Section 44 exempts a farmer, group of farmers or village community from all fees in proceedings before the Authority, Registrar or High Court under the Act or its rules, including document-inspection and copying fees. These provisions reinforce the recognition of farmers as distinct stakeholders in plant variety protection.

Prelims focus

  • Section 39 recognises farmers as breeders, conservers and users of seeds.
  • Farmers may save, sow, resow, exchange, share and sell qualifying farm produce, including seed, under section 39(1)(iv).
  • The exemption does not permit sale of branded seed of a protected variety.
  • Section 26 concerns benefit sharing; section 39(2) concerns failure to meet disclosed seed-performance expectations.
  • Section 45 establishes the National Gene Fund.
  • Trap: Benefit sharing for contributed genetic material is not the same as compensation for seed failing to perform as claimed.

[Sources: India Code, Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001, sections 26 and 39–45, consulted 14 November 2026; Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Authority, Farmers' Rights in the PPV&FR Act, 2001, brochure, sections on access to seed, benefit sharing and compensation; Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Authority, Frequently Asked Questions, question 22 on seed sale and the farmer exemption, revised 23 February 2021; NCERT, Science, Class 8, 'Crop Production and Management', section 1.4, printed pp. 4–5.]

pictures.caption: Farmers help preserve and pass on valuable crop diversity.

pictures.alt: Section 26 links genetic contributions to benefit sharing; Section 39(2) links failure of disclosed seed performance to possible compensation.

title: Farmers' Rights: Seed Saving, Traditional Varieties and Benefit Sharing

body:
What is a trade secret?

A trade secret is information that has commercial value because it is secret and is subject to appropriate efforts to keep it confidential.

Businesses sometimes gain an advantage from methods or information that competitors do not possess. This may involve a recipe, a production process, technical know-how, a commercially useful combination of information or a confidential business method.

The protection concerns the information, not necessarily the visible finished product. A recipe may be confidential even when the food made from it is sold openly. Likewise, a company may keep a particular production method confidential while selling the goods produced by that method.

The 3 core conditions

  • Secrecy: The information is not generally known or readily accessible to people who normally work with that kind of information.
  • Commercial value because of secrecy: Keeping the information confidential provides an actual or potential business advantage.
  • Reasonable protective measures: The rightful holder takes appropriate steps to prevent unauthorised disclosure or use.

Absolute secrecy is not required. More than one trusted employee or business partner may know the information if proper confidentiality obligations and safeguards are maintained. However, information that is already public or easily obtainable in the relevant industry generally cannot be protected merely by describing it as confidential.

Examples of potentially protected information

  • A manufacturer's confidential formula or recipe.
  • Technical know-how used in a production process.
  • Non-public software source code or a commercially valuable technical method.
  • A confidential commercial strategy or combination of business information.
  • Supplier or customer information that genuinely possesses the necessary quality of confidence.

These are possible categories, not automatic legal classifications. An ordinary publicly available customer list, a well-known industrial method or an employee's general professional knowledge does not become a trade secret simply because an employer places a confidentiality label on it.

How businesses maintain confidentiality

Useful practices include limiting access to employees who need the information, using non-disclosure agreements, placing confidentiality obligations in suitable contracts, securing physical records and electronic files, and clearly identifying sensitive materials.

A non-disclosure agreement (NDA) is a contract under which a recipient undertakes not to disclose or misuse specified confidential information. Such agreements can be used with employees, business partners, suppliers or collaborators. Their legal effect depends on the nature of the information, the contractual terms and applicable law.

Duration and registration

Trade secret protection does not require registration in an intellectual property registry. There is also no fixed statutory registration term comparable to a 10-year GI registration. Protection may continue for as long as the information satisfies the necessary conditions, including secrecy.

If information becomes generally known or ceases to be commercially valuable because it is secret, the basis for trade secret protection may disappear. Thus, confidentiality is both the source of the advantage and a condition that must be maintained.

Trade secrets and patents are different

A patent involves a formal legal grant for a qualifying invention, ordinarily requiring disclosure of the invention through the patent system. A trade secret does not require public disclosure, but it also does not provide a patent-like exclusive right against independently developed information.

For a commercially useful manufacturing method, the choice between publication through a patent application and continued secrecy can affect the nature of protection. The existence of a useful method alone does not establish that it qualifies for either form.

Prelims focus

  • A trade secret is commercially valuable information kept confidential.
  • Secrecy, commercial value due to secrecy and reasonable protective steps are the 3 central conditions.
  • Trade secret protection does not require registration.
  • There is no fixed registration term; protection depends on continuing secrecy and the applicable legal requirements.
  • An NDA is one way to establish and maintain a confidentiality obligation.
  • Trap: A confidentiality label cannot make information a trade secret if that information lacks genuine confidentiality.

[Sources: World Intellectual Property Organization, Trade Secrets, sections 'What qualifies as a trade secret?', 'What kind of information is protected?' and 'What kind of protection does a trade secret offer?', consulted 14 November 2026; World Intellectual Property Organization, Frequently Asked Questions: Trade Secrets, sections 'Basics' and 'Requirements for trade secret protection', consulted 14 November 2026; WIPO, Overview of National and Regional Trade Secret Systems: India, sections 1–2, June 2024.]

pictures.caption: A confidential production method may remain valuable because outsiders do not know it.

pictures.alt: Secrecy, commercial value because of secrecy, and reasonable protective steps must combine for trade secret protection; registration is not required.

title: Trade Secrets: Confidential Information as Intellectual Property

body:
How trade secrets are protected in India

As of the 14 November 2026 content cutoff, India does not have a separately enacted, comprehensive trade secrets statute equivalent to the GI Act or PPV&FR Act. Protection mainly arises through contract law and principles concerning breach of confidence. Depending on the conduct, other laws may also apply, such as laws addressing theft or unauthorised access to computer systems.

This position is described in WIPO's India country overview dated June 2024 and the India chapter of the 2026 Intellectual Property practice guide, updated on 10 June 2026. A draft proposal for a separate trade secrets law should not be treated as an enacted statute.

Lawful possession and misuse are different

An employee may legitimately receive confidential technical documents to perform assigned work. The problem arises when the employee improperly copies, discloses or uses protected information contrary to an enforceable obligation of confidence.

A business can reduce this risk through confidentiality clauses, controlled access, clear identification of sensitive documents and procedures for returning records when a working relationship ends. The existence of such measures can also help demonstrate that the information was genuinely treated as confidential.

Employee mobility and professional knowledge

Employees acquire general knowledge, skill and experience through their work. Such ordinary professional abilities are not automatically owned by the former employer as trade secrets.

Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 generally makes agreements restraining a lawful profession, trade or business void to the extent of the restraint, subject to the statutory exception relating to sale of goodwill. As a result, broad restrictions that prevent a former employee from joining a competitor or practising a profession after employment are generally difficult to enforce in India.

This does not mean an employee has unrestricted permission to reveal genuinely confidential information. Courts distinguish a legitimate obligation of confidentiality from an excessive restriction on the employee's ability to work. The precise terms, information and circumstances matter.

General professional skill can normally travel with an employee. Genuinely confidential information obtained under an obligation of confidence cannot simply be copied or disclosed for improper use.

Reverse engineering

Reverse engineering means examining a product to understand how it works or how it was made. For example, a person may study a product lawfully purchased in the market and discover some aspect of its construction or composition.

Trade secret protection generally does not prevent lawful independent discovery or reverse engineering of products legitimately obtained, subject to any other applicable rights and legal obligations. This is a major difference from the exclusive rights created by patents or registered plant variety protection.

However, obtaining confidential drawings from a company's restricted files is not the same as examining a publicly sold product. Unauthorised acquisition or breach of a valid confidence obligation may support a legal claim even when the resulting knowledge concerns a manufacturing method.

Enforcement and remedies

A trade secret holder may seek a civil remedy for breach of contract or breach of confidence. Depending on the facts, the court may grant an injunction to restrain wrongful disclosure or use and may award damages where legally justified.

The claimant must establish the confidential nature of the information, the relevant obligation, and the conduct amounting to misuse or threatened misuse. A civil action for breach of confidence should not be confused with an automatic criminal offence called trade secret infringement. Criminal or information-technology provisions become relevant only when the conduct independently satisfies those laws.

The practical limitation of secrecy

Unlike a registered right that can restrict certain unauthorised commercial acts even after the protected subject becomes publicly identifiable, trade secret protection is vulnerable to lawful discovery. If another business independently develops the same method, the first business generally cannot prohibit that independent use merely because it had previously kept the method secret.

Prelims focus

  • India had no standalone enacted trade secrets statute at the 14 November 2026 content cutoff.
  • Contracts and breach-of-confidence principles are important legal bases for protection.
  • Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 generally restricts enforceability of restraints on lawful trade or profession.
  • General employee skill is different from genuinely confidential employer information.
  • Independent development and lawful reverse engineering generally do not amount to trade secret misuse.
  • Trap: A former employee's work for a competitor is not, by itself, proof of trade secret misappropriation.

[Sources: WIPO, Overview of National and Regional Trade Secret Systems: India, sections 1–4, June 2024, p. 1; Chambers and Partners, Intellectual Property 2026: India, section 5 'Trade Secrets', updated 10 June 2026 and consulted 14 November 2026; WIPO, Trade Secrets, section on independent development and reverse engineering, consulted 14 November 2026; Indian Contract Act, 1872, section 27.]

pictures.alt: Lawful discovery contrasts with copying or disclosure that may misuse confidential information; employee skill and experience are distinct.
pictures.caption: The way information is obtained is central to a trade secret dispute.

title: Trade Secret Enforcement: Contracts, Employees and Reverse Engineering
